n4-aji.meaning_mnemonic: A bite sitting in your <radical>mouth</radical>, chewed but <radical>not yet</radical> gone down, still holds every bit of its <kanji>taste</kanji>.
n4-aji.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a food blogger tries the free onigiri sample and holds the bite on her tongue, humming <reading>み</reading> as if singing <reading>me</reading>, me, only me. She refuses to swallow until she has named every flavour, so the taste just goes on and on while the till beeps.
n4-aji.description: Beyond literal taste, 味 carries the figurative flavour of a thing. It sits inside the common words for 'meaning' and for 'interest', where it points at what something is really like rather than how it tastes on the tongue.

n4-akarui.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> and the <radical>moon</radical> both up in the sky at once leaves the whole valley <kanji>bright</kanji>.
n4-akarui.reading_mnemonic: Outside the gate stands a tourist named May, camera raised at the blinding courtyard. She keeps muttering <reading>めい</reading>, <reading>May</reading>, hunting for the word for bright and finding only her own name, so she just points at the glare instead.

n4-ane.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>woman</radical> trusted to walk to the <radical>market</radical> on her own first is the <kanji>older sister</kanji>.
n4-ane.reading_mnemonic: Back at the river, she silences the squabbling kids with one sharp <reading>し</reading> — a hissed <reading>shh</reading> that cuts through the splashing instantly — the unmistakable sound of an older sister taking charge.
n4-ane.description: Don't confuse this with 妹, the kanji for younger sister. Here the right side stacks a lid over a hanging fold of cloth, a cap over drapery. In 妹 the right side is a tree with an extra short stroke near the top, giving two branches instead of one. Cap-over-cloth is older; two branches is younger.

n4-ani.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>mouth</radical> sitting on top of the tallest pair of <radical>human legs</radical> in the house belongs to your <kanji>older brother</kanji>.
n4-ani.reading_mnemonic: At the school gate, a kid jerks a thumb toward your family and sneers that's <reading>Kay</reading>'s little sibling. Everyone already knows <reading>けい</reading> as the older brother by reputation, before you've said a word.

n4-arau.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Before</radical> any meal you hold your hands under running <radical>water</radical> for a moment, and that first quick rinse is the <kanji>wash</kanji>.
n4-arau.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a laundry-worker called <reading>Sen</reading> scrubs shirts against a flat rock all morning. Each time one comes clean she flings it onto the line and barks <reading>せん</reading> for the next. By noon the rope sags with washed shirts and her throat is raw from shouting it.

n4-asobu.meaning_mnemonic: Drifting like a <radical>swim</radical>mer down whatever <radical>road</radical> opens next, with no place you have to be, is exactly <kanji>play</kanji>.
n4-asobu.reading_mnemonic: After the last bell a kid called <reading>Yu</reading> never walks straight home. His friends stand out on the sports field yelling <reading>ゆう</reading> until he drifts over to whichever game is loudest. One game bleeds into the next, and that is his whole afternoon, every afternoon.

n4-atsumeru.meaning_mnemonic: One <radical>old bird</radical> lands in the <radical>tree</radical> and within a minute the whole flock will <kanji>gather</kanji>.
n4-atsumeru.reading_mnemonic: Up in the branches, an arborist swats at the crowd of old birds and yells <reading>Shoo</reading>, <reading>しゅう</reading>. Not one bird moves off the tree — there are too many, and shooing just isn't going to cut it today.

n4-ba.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sunbeam</radical> breaks through and lands on one square of bare <radical>earth</radical>, and that lit-up patch is now a <kanji>place</kanji> you can point to.
n4-ba.reading_mnemonic: Every morning a hiker called <reading>Joe</reading> climbs to the lone vending machine and plants himself on the exact patch of dirt the sun reaches first. He grunts <reading>じょう</reading> at anyone who edges toward it. That scrap of lit ground is the only spot on the mountain he will call a real place.

n4-betsu.meaning_mnemonic: A single stroke of the <radical>knife</radical> cuts the <radical>wrap</radical> holding the bundle shut, and each hungry <radical>mouth</radical> ends up with a <kanji>separate</kanji> share.
n4-betsu.reading_mnemonic: At the school bake sale a girl called <reading>Betsy</reading> will not pass a tray along until she has sliced it. She saws each slab into portions, muttering <reading>べつ</reading>, almost her own name, at every cut, so no two buyers get the same piece. The wrap ends in a heap and each share leaves on its own plate.
n4-betsu.description: The gloss is 'separate', but 別 just as often means 'another' or 'different', as in a different day or a separate room. Used as a verb with its kun'yomi it means parting from a person: seeing someone off, or breaking up with them.

n4-chi.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Earth</radical> running off flat as a <radical>snake tail</radical> in every direction you look is the <kanji>ground</kanji>.
n4-chi.reading_mnemonic: Still on that trail, a hiker named <reading>Cheech</reading> stubs his toe on the signpost and yelps <reading>ち</reading> — cheese! — hopping backward straight into the motionless snake tail, which doesn't so much as flinch.

n4-chigau.meaning_mnemonic: Every strip of <radical>tanned leather</radical> you <radical>advance</radical> past on the riverbank path is dyed a shade off from the last, so all of them <kanji>differ</kanji>.
n4-chigau.reading_mnemonic: At that same riverbank, a dyer named <reading>Evie</reading> pulls the drying strips down two at a time and holds them up to the sun. The moment a pair does not match, she snaps out a sharp <reading>い</reading> and dunks one straight back in the river.
n4-chigau.description: In everyday speech, the verb form of this kanji often means simply 'no, that's wrong,' not a neutral 'these differ.' Used to answer someone, it corrects them and can sound blunt.

n4-dou.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>One</radical> <radical>mouth</radical> speaking out of a <radical>wide box</radical> makes everybody shut inside it sound the <kanji>same</kanji>.
n4-dou.reading_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, the mouth belongs to the onigiri baker, elbow-deep in <reading>dough</reading> behind the counter. Every time you ask what's going on, he just grunts <reading>どう</reading> without looking up — same shrug, same word, same batch of dough, every single time you ask.

n4-erabu.meaning_mnemonic: Taking the <radical>southeast</radical> <radical>road</radical> when three others were open is exactly what it is to <kanji>choose</kanji>.
n4-erabu.reading_mnemonic: At that same fork, a hiker named <reading>Sen</reading> freezes completely, muttering <reading>せん</reading> over and over while staring at the vending machine, unable to advance a single step until he finally commits to a path.

n4-fueru.meaning_mnemonic: More <radical>earth</radical> on the pile than there was <radical>formerly</radical> is the only proof you need that it will <kanji>increase</kanji>.
n4-fueru.reading_mnemonic: Back at that same signpost, a farmer named Zo watches the water creep higher up the wood and grunts <reading>ぞう</reading> each time — flat and low, like saying '<reading>zo</reading>' with a shrug. By dusk he's grunted it so many times the whole field has crept higher than the post itself.

n4-futoi.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>big</radical> shape with one extra <radical>drop</radical> hanging off the side of it is what we politely call <kanji>fat</kanji>.
n4-futoi.reading_mnemonic: The cook who ladled that stew is a heavyset chef named <reading>Tai</reading>. He pats his own swollen belly, proud of the extra drop he added, and sighs <reading>たい</reading>, satisfied at how thick he's made himself.
n4-futoi.description: 太 is 大 (big) with one extra dot. On 太 that dot sits low, tucked between the legs where the stew dripped in - the mark of something thickened. On 犬 (dog) the dot instead sits high, off the right arm, like a tail flicked up and out. Same big-person shape, different spot for the single drop.

n4-gyou.meaning_mnemonic: Turning the stiff <radical>bristles</radical> you comb off a <radical>sheep</radical> into hairbrushes nailed to a <radical>tree</radical>-stump counter is a strange little <kanji>business</kanji> that somehow pays.
n4-gyou.reading_mnemonic: Koichi liked those sheep-bristle hairbrushes so much he now sells them right by the onigiri shelf, his first real side business. The barcode scanner he calls <reading>Gyo</reading> screeches <reading>ぎょう</reading> each time a brush slides past the beeping till.

n4-hajimeru.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> stepping up onto the <radical>pedestal</radical> is the moment things actually <kanji>begin</kanji>.
n4-hajimeru.reading_mnemonic: The coach doesn't shout 'go' — she just says <reading>し</reading>, flat and clipped like the English word <reading>she</reading>. That single syllable is the starting gun for the dancer, the silkworm, and everyone else still stretching by the lockers.

n4-hakobu.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>army</radical> on the <radical>road</radical> exists mostly to <kanji>carry</kanji> its own supplies from one place to the next.
n4-hakobu.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up, the hiker hauling the cart — everyone just calls her <reading>Oona</reading> — grunts <reading>うん</reading> with every step, the same sound as her own name. At the top, the vending machine rewards her stubbornness with a drink that isn't even the one she wanted.

n4-hashiru.meaning_mnemonic: You break into a <kanji>run</kanji> because the <radical>earth</radical> baking under your shoes will not let you <radical>stop</radical> moving for even one second.
n4-hashiru.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the midday sun turns the dirt to a griddle. A hiker named <reading>Sew</reading> feels it burn through her boots, cannot stand still for even a breath, and sprints for the vending machine at the top, yelping <reading>そう</reading> with every stride.

n4-hataraku.meaning_mnemonic: The one <radical>person</radical> still on the <radical>move</radical> after the whole group has flopped down in the shade is the only one actually doing <kanji>work</kanji>.
n4-hataraku.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she settles in among the cats while the one helper she calls <reading>Dough</reading> sweeps every mossy step, polishes the giant bell, and refills all the lanterns by himself. Each heave on the bell-hammer drags a tired <reading>どう</reading> out of him.
n4-hataraku.description: This is one of a small set of kanji coined in Japan, not borrowed from China. It adds the person radical to the 'move' character, the idea being that a person in motion is a person at work.

n4-hatsu.meaning_mnemonic: Off the blocks, the <radical>outspread legs</radical> explode sideways. The racer's <radical>human legs</radical> land planted wide just as <radical>two</radical> chopsticks clatter off a dropped bento — chasing a train already <kanji>departed</kanji>, hissing steam as it pulls away without them.
n4-hatsu.reading_mnemonic: On the platform, a conductor named <reading>Hatsu</reading> slams the doors and yells <reading>はつ</reading> into his whistle as steam bursts from the wheels — one word, and the train is already gone.

n4-heru-decrease.meaning_mnemonic: Pull the plug in the bathhouse and <radical>all</radical> the <radical>water</radical> races for the drain, so the level can only <kanji>decrease</kanji>.
n4-heru-decrease.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Gen</reading>, the bathhouse attendant, forgets the drain plug every single night. He stands and watches the water sink lower and lower, muttering <reading>げん</reading> as though he is counting each inch it loses. By lock-up the great tub is a shiny empty pit and he is still there saying it.

n4-hiku.meaning_mnemonic: Hooking a straight <radical>stick</radical> behind a <radical>bow</radical>'s string and hauling back until the whole bow bends double is exactly what it means to <kanji>pull</kanji>.
n4-hiku.reading_mnemonic: On the school sports field, the archery captain <reading>Lynn</reading> leans her full weight back against a bow no one else can bend. As she drags the string to her cheek she lets out a strained <reading>いん</reading>, and the team knows that sound means the pull is near breaking point.

n4-hiroi.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>shelter</radical> big enough to lose one small <radical>cocoon</radical> somewhere inside it is genuinely <kanji>wide</kanji>.
n4-hiroi.reading_mnemonic: Koichi surveys his newly renovated konbini — the fluorescent aisles now stretch so wide he needs a golf cart to reach the onigiri shelf. He beams at the beeping till and announces, <reading>こう</reading>, this is what real square footage feels like, pure <reading>Koh</reading>-style efficiency at last.

n4-hitsu.meaning_mnemonic: At the river crossing, a <radical>slash</radical> swinging toward your <radical>heart</radical> makes stepping aside less a choice than a <kanji>necessary</kanji> reflex.
n4-hitsu.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ひつ</reading> is the only word the riverbank ferryman ever says. He will not row you across until you beat him in a quick bout, and the moment his pole taps your chest he spits it out, clipped and flat, sounding just like <reading>hit you</reading>.
n4-hitsu.description: The look-alike is 心, heart or mind. 心 is the bare heart shape, a wide low curve with three loose dots and nothing crossing it. 必 adds one straight slash cutting from the upper right down through the middle, and that diagonal is the whole difference.

n4-hitsuji.meaning_mnemonic: This one is a gift, because the <radical>sheep</radical> radical and the <kanji>sheep</kanji> kanji are the very same character.
n4-hitsuji.reading_mnemonic: A single sheep has planted itself in the middle of the mountain trail and will not move. Every time a hiker tries to edge past, it lifts its head and gives one flat <reading>よう</reading>, a greeting so bored it lands somewhere between a warning and a mumbled <reading>yo</reading>.

n4-hosoi.meaning_mnemonic: Someone stretches one strand of <radical>thread</radical> across the whole <radical>rice field</radical>. Pulled taut over that distance, the strand thins more with every step. By the far edge it is nearly invisible, worn <kanji>thin</kanji>.
n4-hosoi.reading_mnemonic: Farmer <reading>Sai</reading> walks the paddy edge every morning, running a finger along the line to find it. Each time he loses sight of it in the grass he mutters <reading>さい</reading>, annoyed at how thin the thing is.

n4-hou.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>direction</radical> radical and the <kanji>direction</kanji> kanji are the same, and it also works as a polite word for a person, since pointing someone's way is a soft way to point them out.
n4-hou.reading_mnemonic: Where the shrine path splits three ways, an old gardener leans on his <reading>hoe</reading> and never says a word. Ask him which fork to take and he simply swings the hoe to point down one of them with a low, breathy <reading>ほう</reading>.
n4-hou.description: The look-alike is 万, ten thousand. 万 has one flat top line, only three strokes, and a last stroke that sweeps far out to the lower left. 方 adds a short cap stroke above the top line and a crossbar through the middle, and its hooked last stroke stays short and tucked in.

n4-ie-kanji.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>pig</radical> living under your <radical>roof</radical> is what makes the place a <kanji>house</kanji> instead of a barn.
n4-ie-kanji.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches on the power line outside that house, unimpressed by the racket inside. Every time the pig squeals and kicks at the ceiling, she tips her head back and lets out one <reading>か</reading> — a dry little <reading>kah</reading> of judgment. Then she goes back to smoking her own beak.

n4-imouto.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> who is <radical>not yet</radical> old enough for anyone to call her one is the <kanji>younger sister</kanji> of the house.
n4-imouto.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine a toddler chases every cat down the mossy steps, grabbing fur and howling <reading>my</reading>, my, mine, which comes out of her as <reading>まい</reading>. She is too little to know the shrine cats belong to no one. Grandma Kane scoops her up before she reaches the big bell.
n4-imouto.description: The look-alike is 姉, 'older sister'. Both share the 'woman' element on the left, so the difference is all on the right. 妹 has 'not yet': a tree with two crossbars, the upper shorter, and two short diagonals flaring out at the foot like roots. 姉 instead has a small tick atop a boxy cloth shape, with one long vertical dropping straight through and out the bottom, and no flaring feet.

n4-iro.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody down in a <radical>crouch</radical> over a <radical>swirl</radical> of dye is mixing up one more <kanji>color</kanji>.
n4-iro.reading_mnemonic: A dye-shop apprentice grabs the vat's exposed wire without thinking and gets a jolt of <reading>shock</reading>, yelping <reading>しょく</reading> as sparks scatter across the wet, rainbow-streaked threads still steaming on the table.

n4-isogu.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>snout</radical> at your back and your <radical>heart</radical> down in a <radical>crouch</radical> is all the reason anybody needs to <kanji>hurry</kanji>.
n4-isogu.reading_mnemonic: Skidding into that same hallway, a courier pigeon named <reading>Cue</reading> can't stop in time and slams into the pile, wheezing out a strangled <reading>きゅう</reading> as crumbs and feathers go flying. He's always this late, and it's always this loud.

n4-ji-self.meaning_mnemonic: You get this one for free, because the <radical>self</radical> radical you already know and the <kanji>self</kanji> kanji are the exact same character.
n4-ji-self.reading_mnemonic: A genie drifts up from the offering box at Grandma Kane's shrine, and when you ask who he takes orders from, he points a finger straight at his own nose and says <reading>じ</reading>. It comes out like a flat <reading>Gee</reading>, the sound you make when the answer was always going to be yourself.
n4-ji-self.description: All three are a tall box with inner lines. 自 has a short slanted stroke on top and two inner lines, splitting it into three parts. 目, eye, has those same three parts but no stroke on top. 白, white, has the top stroke but only one inner line, so it splits into two.

n4-kai.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> who walks the trail head-down and a <radical>cloud</radical> parked at face height are bound to <kanji>meet</kanji> with a soft, damp bump.
n4-kai.reading_mnemonic: Up where the trail vanishes into low cloud, a hiker named <reading>Kai</reading> has set up beside the one vending machine. Every climber who finally reaches him calls out <reading>かい</reading>, so his name is also the sound two people make when they meet.
n4-kai.description: 会 and 今 share the same wide, person-shaped lid on top. Under the lid, 会, meet, carries a full boxy shape with a bar across it and more strokes stacked below. 今, now, has almost nothing under the lid, just one short hooked stroke like a tiny 7 and no bar.

n4-kangaeru.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>old</radical> man with a permanent <radical>kink</radical> in his back has nothing but time to sit and <kanji>think</kanji>.
n4-kangaeru.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, spots the old man frozen mid-crosswalk and can't restock the onigiri shelf until he moves. A crow on the awning tips its head and <reading>caws</reading> — <reading>こう</reading> — the exact sound of someone thinking too hard to hurry.

n4-kariru.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> walking off with what they need today and putting off paying it back until it feels like <radical>once upon a time</radical> is how you <kanji>borrow</kanji>.
n4-kariru.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, borrows a rickety <reading>shack</reading> from the person down the road and never gives it back. Every time the owner comes asking, Kaa just croaks <reading>しゃく</reading> from the power line and singes the eviction notice to ash.
n4-kariru.description: 借 covers renting as much as borrowing — money, an apartment, a bike, anything you take now and promise to give back or pay for. English splits borrow and rent; this kanji does both.

n4-karui.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>holy</radical> hand laid flat on a loaded <radical>vehicle</radical> draws the weight out like a blessing, until the <kanji>light (weight)</kanji> cart drifts a finger off the road.
n4-karui.reading_mnemonic: A kid named <reading>Kay</reading> runs after the blessed cart as it drifts down the road a finger off the ground. Every time it bobs higher she shouts <reading>けい</reading>, which is her own name and the exact sound Japanese gives the letter K.

n4-kasu.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>lend</kanji> by handing your <radical>money</radical> to a <radical>substitute</radical> owner who stands in your place and must return every coin.
n4-kasu.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, guards a pile of coins on the power line above Koichi's konbini and only lends to people who look smart. You knot a proper <reading>tie</reading> at your neck, so he leans down, croaks <reading>たい</reading>, singes the knot to mark it, and drops the loan in your hands.

n4-kawaru.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>trailing foot</radical> that turns up <radical>also</radical> on the far side of the room means something did <kanji>change</kanji>.
n4-kawaru.reading_mnemonic: Watching this spin from the doorway, a chicken named <reading>Hen</reading> squawks <reading>へん</reading> in pure disbelief, the same flat sound as her own name. The duckling waddles off wearing the pot lid like a crown.
n4-kawaru.description: This kanji doubles as a common na-adjective meaning strange or odd, not just change — context decides which sense is meant, and native speakers reach for that second sense constantly.

n4-kei-pass.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>thread</radical> of <radical>holy</radical> writing you have to follow line by line is how you <kanji>pass through</kanji> a sutra.
n4-kei-pass.reading_mnemonic: The apprentice threading the loom is named <reading>Kay</reading>. Every time the shuttle passes through she exhales a low <reading>けい</reading>, matching the monk's chant beat for beat, until the thread and the sutra finish the row together.

n4-ken-exam.meaning_mnemonic: Trotting one <radical>horse</radical> up and down in front of the whole <radical>assembly</radical> is how they <kanji>examine</kanji> it.
n4-ken-exam.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting dog, guards the clinic door with a wall of antique blades gleaming behind him. Every time the horse tries to bolt past without finishing its checkup, Ken barks one sharp <reading>けん</reading> — <reading>Ken</reading> means nobody skips the exam.

n4-kimeru.meaning_mnemonic: Once the <radical>water</radical> has broken the bank it has already <radical>decide</radical>d for you, so you may as well <kanji>decide</kanji> too.
n4-kimeru.reading_mnemonic: Perched on the signpost, a marmot named Ketch watches the paint drip and chitters <reading>けつ</reading>, <reading>Ketch</reading>, approving her choice before scrambling down the now-legible path ahead of her.

n4-kiru-wear.meaning_mnemonic: Cut one <radical>slash</radical> down a whole <radical>sheep</radical>, pull the fleece around you until it hides an <radical>eye</radical>, and you <kanji>wear</kanji> the animal itself.
n4-kiru-wear.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, giggles inside her old oak while you wrestle into the fresh sheep-fleece coat. She pokes a branch out and gives the hem one hard <reading>chuck</reading> downward to seat it on your shoulders, laughing <reading>ちゃく</reading> as the collar flops over your eyes.
n4-kiru-wear.description: One character, two senses that feel unrelated: to put on or wear clothing, and to arrive at or reach a place. The wear sense uses the kun reading; the arrive sense shows up in travel words for arrival and landing. It is normal to be thrown that the same character means both.

n4-kotae.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>bamboo</radical> slip that happens to <radical>fit</radical> the empty slot exactly is the <kanji>answer</kanji>.
n4-kotae.reading_mnemonic: Sei stubs her toe on the bamboo root right where the ground cracked open, and yelps instead of answering the teacher's question. Everyone laughs, but the barked <reading>とう</reading> still counts — a stubbed <reading>toe</reading> makes exactly that sound, and gets treated as her answer anyway.

n4-koto.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>matter</kanji> is whatever an animal's <radical>snout</radical> has pinned to the <radical>ground</radical> and its <radical>mouth</radical> has sunk a <radical>barb</radical> into, so it can never be dropped.
n4-koto.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a fisherman hooks something huge, and each time the line jerks he grunts <reading>じ</reading>, which is just <reading>gee</reading> with the air knocked out of him. Whatever it is has swallowed the barb and will not shake loose, so it is his problem now, dragging him through the mud.
n4-koto.description: The 'thing' here is always an intangible one: a matter, an affair, an event, something that happens or that you have to deal with. A physical object you can pick up is a different word entirely. With its kun'yomi it is the ordinary spoken word for an abstract 'thing'.

n4-kuraberu.meaning_mnemonic: You get this one for free, because the <radical>compare</radical> radical and the <kanji>compare</kanji> kanji are the very same character, so it pays to know your radicals well.
n4-kuraberu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank a heron named Hina lays two fish side by side to compare their weight. A jogger asks who landed the bigger one, so Hina jabs her beak toward the old fisherman, meaning <reading>he</reading> did, and croaks a flat <reading>ひ</reading> to settle it.

n4-kurai.meaning_mnemonic: A room with its <radical>sun</radical> switched off, where you steer only by <radical>sound</radical>, is the very definition of <kanji>dark</kanji>.
n4-kurai.reading_mnemonic: Ann, the mole, shuffles across the pitch-black room feeling along the wall until she finds the switch marked <reading>on</reading>. She flicks it again and again and nothing happens, so she groans <reading>あん</reading> and goes back to steering by sound in the total dark.

n4-kyou-teach.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>teach</kanji> is to drill <radical>filial piety</radical> into a child with one bamboo <radical>tap</radical> until propping the old man upright feels natural.
n4-kyou-teach.reading_mnemonic: At the school, the cane-happy teacher everyone calls <reading>Kyo</reading> opens each lesson by making you haul a sandbag 'grandpa' across the field. Every time he barks your name, you chant <reading>きょう</reading> straight back at him.

n4-mise.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>shelter</radical> on the corner doing <radical>fortune-telling</radical> for cash is still, legally speaking, a <kanji>shop</kanji>.
n4-mise.reading_mnemonic: A customer ducks through the yawning mouth-shaped doorway and drops <reading>ten</reading> coins on the tortoise's card table. He gets his fortune shouted back in one flat syllable, <reading>てん</reading>, then returns every week for the same price.

n4-modoru.meaning_mnemonic: Anything <radical>big</radical> enough to shove the never-latching <radical>door</radical> can <kanji>return</kanji> to the konbini heater whenever it wants.
n4-modoru.reading_mnemonic: That big stray dog is called <reading>Ray</reading>. However many times Koichi shoos him out, the never-latching door swings open and lets him trot back past the onigiri shelf to the heater. Koichi just sighs <reading>れい</reading> and refills the food bowl.
n4-modoru.description: The backtracking sense of return: going back where you were or putting something back, not returning home.

n4-mono.meaning_mnemonic: Anybody who has stood in enough <radical>sun</radical> to go <radical>old</radical> under it is a <kanji>person</kanji> worth asking.
n4-mono.reading_mnemonic: The driver stuck idling at that crosswalk, a man named <reading>Shuji</reading>, finally leans on his horn and shouts <reading>しゃ</reading> — shoo! The shuffling old figure doesn't even glance up, finishing the crossing at exactly the same pace.
n4-mono.description: 者 almost never stands alone as a word; it works as a suffix stitched onto a verb or field to name whoever does it, much the way English -er turns 'teach' into 'teacher'. Learning it as a floating idea of a person is the right starting point, but expect to meet it glued onto the end of something else far more often than by itself.

n4-motsu.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>hand</radical> that can <kanji>hold</kanji> an entire <radical>Buddhist temple</radical> down on its measured plot of ground has a grip that never slips.
n4-motsu.reading_mnemonic: At the temple, the old monk makes you hold the huge bronze bell over your head while he counts the yard stones. Soon your arms shake so hard that the only sound you manage is <reading>じ</reading>. It is the flat <reading>gee</reading> anyone groans under a weight they cannot put down.
n4-motsu.description: In its continuous form it also means to have or own, so possessing a car or a pet counts as hold too.

n4-narau.meaning_mnemonic: A young bird beating one <radical>white</radical> <radical>feather</radical> against the air over and over is trying hard to <kanji>learn</kanji>.
n4-narau.reading_mnemonic: A birdwatcher named Shoe sits on the bank with a clipboard, tally marks climbing with every failed launch. She murmurs <reading>しゅう</reading>, <reading>Shoe</reading> under her breath at each attempt, certain the duckling will get airborne if it just keeps practicing.

n4-nokoru.meaning_mnemonic: After the <radical>bad luck</radical> has come and gone there are only <radical>shallow</radical> scratches left, and those <kanji>remain</kanji>.
n4-nokoru.reading_mnemonic: Every morning the shrine's groundskeeper cat, a stubborn old tom named <reading>Zan</reading>, sniffs at the broken halberd and grumbles <reading>ざん</reading>, deciding again it isn't his job to move it — so there it stays.

n4-oboeru.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>remember</kanji> a <radical>small</radical> fact by tucking it under a <radical>cover</radical> where your roving eye can still <radical>see</radical> the lump it makes.
n4-oboeru.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine, Grandma Kane keeps the one phone number she still needs tucked under a sleeping cat's blanket. Each time she lifts the cover, checks it, and finds she still knows it, she gives a dry <reading>かく</reading>. That is the small <reading>cackle</reading> of someone glad her mind still works.
n4-oboeru.description: The active side of remember, closer to memorize or learn by heart than to passive recall.

n4-okuru.meaning_mnemonic: Walking somebody as far as the <radical>frontier gate</radical> and no further down the <radical>road</radical> is how you <kanji>send</kanji> them off.
n4-okuru.reading_mnemonic: The boy's only witness is Sow, a pig who lives by the crossing. Every time he lobs a parcel over the water, she gives the same unimpressed grunt, <reading>そう</reading>. It sounds exactly like someone muttering <reading>so</reading> to themselves, right before they let something go.

n4-omoi.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>village</radical> told to shift a <radical>thousand</radical> rice sacks finds out fast that a thousand of anything at once is too <kanji>heavy</kanji> to move.
n4-omoi.reading_mnemonic: The village hires a furniture mover named <reading>Jude</reading> to bring its thousand rice sacks up from the riverbank in one load. He gets three sacks onto his back, sinks to his knees in the mud, and stays there groaning <reading>じゅう</reading> until the tide comes in.
n4-omoi.description: The one to watch is 車 (car / vehicle). 車 is symmetrical: one upright stroke runs straight down through a single boxed grid, with a short bar above and below. 重 breaks that balance. Its top has a slanted lid stroke, and an extra horizontal bar cuts across the full width partway down. The widest line sits at the very bottom, so the whole character looks low and bottom-heavy.

n4-omou.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>rice field</radical> sitting on your <radical>heart</radical> all winter is what keeps a farmer awake to <kanji>think</kanji>.
n4-omou.reading_mnemonic: A heron named Shi stands dead still over the rice field, chewing over something enormous. Every few minutes it snaps its beak and lets out one flat <reading>し</reading> — proof that all that stillness is <reading>Shi</reading>'s thought, not sleep.

n4-otouto.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Split</radical> the inheritance, offer <radical>condolences</radical>, and one <radical>slash</radical> of the pen leaves the <kanji>younger brother</kanji> nothing.
n4-otouto.reading_mnemonic: That same reckless kid trips over his own tangled bowstring and yelps <reading>Tay</reading>, <reading>てい</reading>, don't tell mom, already looping a second cord before anyone can drag him back inside for dinner.

n4-owaru.meaning_mnemonic: The last <radical>thread</radical> runs out at exactly the moment <radical>winter</radical> arrives, and that is the <kanji>end</kanji>.
n4-owaru.reading_mnemonic: The instant the thread runs out, one of the shrine cats pounces on the duckling's lace. It clamps its teeth down like it's stealing a <reading>shoe</reading>. Its triumphant yowl comes out as <reading>しゅう</reading> — the exact sound of the last stretch of thread giving way.

n4-oya.meaning_mnemonic: At the edge of Sei's school field, someone has climbed a <radical>tree</radical> and wedged themselves to <radical>stand</radical> on the highest branch. They crane forward to <radical>see</radical> every second of the match without missing a kick. That straining figure, who won't leave until it's over, is a <kanji>parent</kanji>.
n4-oya.reading_mnemonic: When the final whistle blows, they scramble down too fast and bark their <reading>しん</reading> — their <reading>shin</reading> — hard against a branch, then limp off still cheering about the goal.

n4-ri.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>king</radical> explaining his rules to one small <radical>village</radical> has to fall back on plain <kanji>logic</kanji>.
n4-ri.reading_mnemonic: A surveyor named <reading>Reeko</reading> stands where the king planted his spike, snapping her measuring cord taut across the paddies with a sharp <reading>り</reading> every time a farmer's row drifts off the straight line.

n4-ryou-fee.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody has to <radical>measure</radical> out the <radical>rice</radical>, and what they charge you for doing it is the <kanji>fee</kanji>.
n4-ryou-fee.reading_mnemonic: A customer named <reading>Leo</reading> counts each dipper-load of rice as it clinks into his bag, muttering <reading>りょう</reading>, <reading>りょう</reading>. He keeps track of how many scoops he owes, until his tally and the register's total match up, scoop for scoop.

n4-sha.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>cult</radical> that owns a patch of <radical>earth</radical> and a gate onto the road has become a <kanji>shrine</kanji>.
n4-sha.reading_mnemonic: Still behind the shrine, a new hire named <reading>Shae</reading> trips over the freshly staked signpost and yelps <reading>しゃ</reading>. She stumbles face-first into the altar's offering tray — her first day at the company already the stuff of legend.
n4-sha.description: 社 originally named the local earth god's shrine — the altar raised on a patch of claimed ground for a village's protector spirit. The word later stretched to cover any group organized around a shared institution, which is why it equally means a shrine and a company: the modern sense kept the idea of a formal body bound to a place, not the religious content.

n4-shi-try.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> delivered in exactly the right <radical>style</radical> are what they are listening for when they <kanji>try</kanji> you.
n4-shi-try.reading_mnemonic: A foreman named <reading>Shii</reading> paces around the ceremony, hissing a stressed <reading>し</reading> through his teeth every time the speech wobbles. He's sure the whole shaky test is about to collapse before the stake settles into the ground.

n4-shin-heart.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>heart</radical> radical and the <kanji>heart</kanji> kanji are one and the same, and because old Japanese placed thought in the chest rather than the head, the shape also means mind.
n4-shin-heart.reading_mnemonic: Shin the jogger stops at Grandma Kane's shrine every morning to complain about his <reading>しん</reading>, his aching <reading>shin</reading>. One morning a cat on the mossy steps trips him, and the fall finally gives his hammering heart something else to worry about.
n4-shin-heart.description: The one to watch is 必 (necessary). Both have the same curved, swooping base and a scatter of short dots, but 必 drives a straight diagonal stroke right through the center of the shape, running down toward the lower left. 心 has nothing crossing it: just the open curved base and three separate dots resting around it. If a line spears through the middle, you are looking at 必, not 心.

n4-shinu.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Bad luck</radical> and a <radical>spoon</radical> where a knife should have been is how most people quietly <kanji>die</kanji>.
n4-shinu.reading_mnemonic: Behind the register at Koichi's konbini, the cashier named <reading>She</reading> hears the crash and doesn't even look up, just breathes one flat <reading>し</reading> and rings up the shattered tub anyway. Nothing about tonight is going to surprise her.

n4-shiraberu.meaning_mnemonic: Carrying <radical>words</radical> the full <radical>circumference</radical> of the village is how you <kanji>investigate</kanji> anything at all.
n4-shiraberu.reading_mnemonic: Behind the register stands a beat cop named Chow, notebook open, tallying every stacked bubble. He grunts <reading>ちょう</reading>, <reading>Chow</reading>, each time a suspect's story shifts, until his tally points straight at the onigiri thief hiding behind the till.

n4-shiru.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, an <radical>arrow</radical> streaks across the grass and thunks dead center into the target. In that same instant, your <radical>mouth</radical> snaps open with the answer, just the fact flying out as fast and true as the shot. That instant, certain hit is <kanji>knowing</kanji> something.
n4-shiru.reading_mnemonic: Chibi the parrot roosts on that same target and shrieks <reading>ち</reading> the second the arrow lands, confirming the answer before you can even say it out loud — a sharp <reading>chee</reading> of certainty every time.

n4-shitsu.meaning_mnemonic: The first place you <radical>arrive</radical> at once you are under a <radical>roof</radical> is a <kanji>room</kanji>.
n4-shitsu.reading_mnemonic: A landlady everyone calls <reading>Shitsu</reading> stomps in to inspect the new room. She presses her ear to the dart quivering in the floorboards and grunts a flat <reading>しつ</reading> of approval. Then she stamps the doorframe and moves to the next one.

n4-shitsu-quality.meaning_mnemonic: Testing a coin of <radical>money</radical> against the flat back of an <radical>axe</radical> is a fast check on its <kanji>quality</kanji>.
n4-shitsu-quality.reading_mnemonic: The peddler pockets one more coin, but stump sawdust dusts his palm and it starts to itch. Sheesh, itchy, he hisses, shaking his hand out and blowing grit off the last coin, muttering <reading>しつ</reading>, <reading>しつ</reading> — the sound comes out exactly like his <reading>itchy</reading> complaint.

n4-shu-main.meaning_mnemonic: Put a <radical>lid</radical> on top of the <radical>king</radical> and whatever ends up sitting above him is the <kanji>main</kanji> thing.
n4-shu-main.reading_mnemonic: Back on the throne, the king's valet holds up the lord's one remaining polished <reading>shoe</reading> and announces <reading>しゅ</reading> to the court. The shoe proves who's still the main one in charge, wax-sealed crown and all.
n4-shu-main.description: 主 differs from 王 by exactly one mark: 主 adds a small drop stroke sitting above the top horizontal line, before the three stacked bars begin, while 王 has no dot at all — just the three flat crowns and the single spike through the middle, nothing above the topmost bar.

n4-suki.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> with her own <radical>child</radical> is the one pairing everybody in the room is expected to <kanji>like</kanji>.
n4-suki.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, watches from the till and tries to <reading>coax</reading> the toddler back with a sticker, murmuring <reading>こう</reading>, <reading>こう</reading>. But the kid's already found someone better to hug, so Koichi just restocks the onigiri instead.

n4-tobu.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>fly</radical> radical and the <kanji>fly</kanji> kanji are the same character, a point you earn just by knowing your radicals.
n4-tobu.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Hina</reading> the hang-glider pilot shoves off from the top of the mountain trail, sure she will soar this time. She clips the lone vending machine on the way past and drifts down going <reading>ひ</reading>, a long thin wheeze, before the bushes catch her.

n4-todoku.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>body</radical> at your door with a good <radical>reason</radical> to be there is how parcels <kanji>deliver</kanji> themselves.
n4-todoku.reading_mnemonic: At the same party, a courier named <reading>Kai</reading> keeps sighing <reading>かい</reading> as he hauls yet another box across the tatami to the body's leg. He's resigned to the fact that delivery here always means dragging, never handing.

n4-tokoro.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>door</radical> and the <radical>axe</radical> hung on the wall beside it mark out one particular <kanji>place</kanji>.
n4-tokoro.reading_mnemonic: A mailman circles the stump twice before he's sure, then stamps the address form with one flat syllable, <reading>しょ</reading>, like he's about to <reading>show</reading> you exactly where to stand, axe and swinging door included.

n4-tsukau.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> the <radical>officer</radical> can send anywhere at an hour's notice is one he will <kanji>use</kanji> constantly.
n4-tsukau.reading_mnemonic: Shiba the heron struts along that same riverbank, screeching orders of his own at the laundry crew like a tiny drill sergeant. The sound comes out as a piercing <reading>し</reading>, pure <reading>sheesh</reading>, every single time someone slacks off scrubbing.

n4-tsuyoi.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>bow</radical> strung with silk from a single <radical>cocoon</radical> can still put an arrow through an <radical>insect</radical>, which is <kanji>strong</kanji>.
n4-tsuyoi.reading_mnemonic: Back in the locker room, a boy named <reading>Kyo</reading> stares at the bent bow and mutters <reading>きょう</reading>, きょう, over and over, unable to believe a beetle just out-arm-wrestled the entire soccer team.

n4-tsuzukeru.meaning_mnemonic: As long as there is <radical>thread</radical> left to <radical>sell</radical>, the market will happily <kanji>continue</kanji>.
n4-tsuzukeru.reading_mnemonic: At those same shrine steps, a tourist named <reading>Zach</reading> tries to leave but his legs won't quit marching in place, round and round. Every stomp echoes <reading>ぞく</reading> off the mossy stone, on and on, refusing to stop.

n4-uta.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>song</kanji> is what you get when your <radical>big brother</radical> starts a <radical>yawn</radical> so wide that it turns into a tune halfway through.
n4-uta.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow lands on the power line above the school field to join the children's singing. Every time she opens her beak, the note comes out as a burnt <reading>か</reading>. It is a <reading>caw</reading> with a puff of flame that scorches the grass below.

n4-warui.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>heart</radical> big enough to want all of <radical>Asia</radical> for itself has gone thoroughly <kanji>bad</kanji>.
n4-warui.reading_mnemonic: The cat, still hissing, gets its tail pinned under a fallen bin and yowls in pure <reading>awkward</reading> pain — <reading>あく</reading> — echoing off the shrine steps before it slinks away, guiltier than ever.

n4-wasureru.meaning_mnemonic: When a name you loved slips under the lid and joins the <radical>deceased</radical>, your <radical>heart</radical> keeps beating but you <kanji>forget</kanji> it was ever there.
n4-wasureru.reading_mnemonic: An old classmate waves at you on the mossy shrine steps, and you have completely forgotten his name. You stall with a slow, deep <reading>bow</reading>, your back creaking <reading>ぼう</reading> as it sinks. He bows back just as lost, and the shrine cats watch two grown adults <reading>ぼう</reading>-ing in silence, neither one admitting he forgot.

n4-you-need.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>flat lid</radical> and one <radical>woman</radical> who knows where everything lives are all any kitchen will ever <kanji>need</kanji>.
n4-you-need.reading_mnemonic: Backstage, the stage manager keeps checking his clipboard and groaning <reading>よう</reading>, the same sound he'd make chasing a lost <reading>yo-yo</reading> under the bleachers. The dancer still hasn't shown up, and the whole show needs her.

n4-yowai.meaning_mnemonic: An archer's <radical>bow</radical> catches a coating of <radical>ice</radical> on a cold morning. She pulls back, but the frozen string barely bends. It snaps loose with no power at all, proving how <kanji>weak</kanji> the bow has become.
n4-yowai.reading_mnemonic: Halfway down that same icy trail, a hiker named <reading>Jock</reading> collapses against a boulder, legs shaking, and moans <reading>じゃく</reading>, じゃく, over and over. The frozen bow slides out of his numb fingers into the snow.

n4-zoku.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>clan</kanji> is everyone who aims an <radical>arrow</radical> in whatever <radical>direction</radical> the <radical>chevron</radical> at the top of the war banner is tilted.
n4-zoku.reading_mnemonic: Uncle <reading>Zock</reading> has made himself head of the whole clan and lines every cousin up behind his banner on the mountain trail. A gust off the peak sends a shudder down the family, <reading>ぞく</reading>, <reading>ぞく</reading>, one relative after the next. He won't break formation, so the shivering just loops back to the front.
n4-zoku.description: This character almost never stands alone. It works as a suffix on the end of a compound, marking a group bound by blood or by kind: a household, a tribe, an ethnic people, a band of nobles. Read it as 'the ... folk' rather than a word you say by itself.

n4-zu.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Mow</radical> one <radical>small</radical> path across an <radical>enclosure</radical> and you have drawn your first <kanji>map</kanji>.
n4-zu.reading_mnemonic: A surveyor called <reading>Zuzu</reading> gets called in to examine the scratched walls. She traces one finger along the lines and grunts a single <reading>ず</reading> of approval — first map she's ever seen that doubles as a cry for help.
